newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BA offers talks as cabin crew set strike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BA offers talks as cabin crew set strike.

text.p: British Airways Plc moved to avert a summer of discontent for holidaymakers on Tuesday in an apparent climbdown offer of peace talks with cabin crew after union bosses backed a series of strikes starting next week.

Bill Morris, general secretary of the Transport & General Workers Union (T&G) -- the union leading the dispute talks -- made the final decision to sanction strike action late on Tuesday after failing to tempt BA into talks with cabin crew earlier in the day.

But as soon as the T&G announced a series of 72-hour strikes would begin next week after continued deadlock over the cabin crew pay row, BA chief executive Bob Ayling announced he was writing to Morris asking for talks under the supervision of an independent arbitrator.
Ayling said in his letter that such an approach had been successful in ending the pilots' dispute last year.
"Why don't we adopt the same approach for BA/cabin crew relations?" said Ayling in his letter.
BA added that he was also confident of reaching agreement with ground staff within 48 hours over their grievances involving the sale of BA's catering unit.
The T&G was unavailable for an immediate response to the BA peace offering.
But Morris had said in a statement earlier that it had no choice but to back strike action.

"Since BA have turned a deaf ear to common sense, the union is left with no choice but to authorise the action requested by BA employees. Strike action will therefore be taken next week after the required period of seven days notice has elapsed," he said.
The strike marks the start of the first serious industrial relations dispute since the Labour government was elected on May 1.

Next week's strikes will be held by BA cabin crew over a five-month-long pay row. Three quarters of cabin crew were balloted by the T&G last week over whether to take strike action, and 73 percent of those balloted said 'yes'.

The decision to press ahead with a spate of 72 hour stoppages was taken after BA's Ayling reiterated earlier on Tuesday that he would not enter talks until cabin crew renounced their "militancy". That position now appears to have changed.
BA had already said it was prepared to talk to ground staff over a separate row over the sale of BA's catering unit.
On Monday, 62 percent of ground staff balloted voted to back a strike. Ground staff met earlier on Tuesday to decide whether they would follow cabin crew colleagues down the path of confrontation.
If they decide to follow, BA faces a momentous problem on ground and in the air.
Both disputes stem from BA's restructuring efforts to cull one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) from costs by the year 2000.
Analysts warned the cost of strike will be onerous on BA profitability unless a last-ditch reprieve is gained.
"A strike would make a massive difference to BA -- financially in the short term as well as hurting it long term," said Chris Avery, analyst at Paribas earlier this week.
Industry observers pointed out that just the threat of a BA pilots' strike last year wiped more than 10 million pounds off group profits as passengers switched to other airlines.
BA's services from both Heathrow -- Europe's busiest airport -- and Gatwick will be hit.

The airline has already put its operations on red alert by retraining managers to take on extra roles, taken on extra security and set aside resources for taxis, coaches and hotels for strike breakers to break the picket lines.
It has warned potential strikers that they face the sack or legal action at worst and loss of promotion and benefits, triggering union accusations of "intimidation and terrorism."

Such was the determination of BA's Ayling to face down the union threat that he cancelled his trip to witness the handover of Hong Kong on Monday, warning BA would not bow down to "1970s style trade unionism." ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
